mainEntity.name: How much does a car depreciate in five years?

acceptedAnswer.text: A common rule of thumb is around 40% to 60% for a new car, depending on the model. This calculator's typical curve loses about 50% over five years for a midsize SUV, but individual vehicles vary widely.

mainEntity.name: Which cars hold their value best?

acceptedAnswer.text: Trucks and some popular SUVs tend to keep more value, while luxury sedans and many electric vehicles have lost more. Reliability, fuel prices, incentives and new model launches all move the market.

mainEntity.name: Is it cheaper to buy used?

acceptedAnswer.text: Often, because the first owner pays for the steepest depreciation. Use the condition setting to see the effect, but include the cost of any extra maintenance an older car needs.
Yes. Higher mileage lowers resale value and can accelerate wear. This tool uses your mileage to work out cost per mile; for a precise resale value, compare listings with similar mileage.

mainEntity.name: What is total cost of ownership?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is everything that leaving the car in your driveway costs over the time you own it: the value it loses, loan interest, insurance, maintenance, fuel and other running costs, less nothing you get back except the resale value.

mainEntity.name: How do you calculate car depreciation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Multiply the starting value by (1 − yearly rate) for each year. A $30,000 car losing 15% a year is worth about $18,424 after 3 years and $13,311 after 5.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between straight-line and declining balance depreciation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Straight-line removes the same dollar amount every year. Declining balance removes a percentage of the current value, so losses shrink over time. For a $30,000 car at 15% over 5 years the results are $7,500 and $13,311.

mainEntity.name: How do I find my car's annual depreciation rate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use rate = 1 − (resale value ÷ purchase price)^(1 ÷ years). A $30,000 car worth $15,000 after 5 years lost about 12.9% a year.

mainEntity.name: How long does it take a car to lose half its value?

acceptedAnswer.text: About 4.3 years at 15% a year, 3.1 years at 20% and 6.6 years at 10%.

mainEntity.name: What is negative equity on a car loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: It means you owe more than the car is worth. With no down payment and an 84-month loan on a $38,500 car, you could be about $2,403 underwater after one year.

mainEntity.name: Does car depreciation slow down over time?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The dollar loss is largest in the first years and shrinks. On a $38,500 car the calculator's typical curve loses $6,930 in year 1 and $2,174 in year 5.

mainEntity.name: Is it cheaper to buy a new or a used car, depreciation-wise?

acceptedAnswer.text: A car two years old has already lost the steepest part of its value. On the typical curve a $38,500 car loses about $11,665 (30%) in the first two years and about $7,272 over the next three.

mainEntity.name: Is car depreciation the same as tax depreciation?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. This tool estimates resale value. Tax depreciation for business vehicles follows different schedules.
